claims.text: Conventionally processed W–Cu composites contain tungsten–copper interfaces formed during sintering.
Cu modification of tungsten-particle surfaces can form seamless, ultra-stable heterointerfaces between tungsten and copper.
The Cu-modified interface improves bonding between the tungsten and copper phases.
The Cu-modified interface enhances electron and phonon coupling between tungsten and copper.
A seamless, well-bonded W–Cu interface reduces thermal contact resistance at tungsten–copper phase boundaries.
Reduced interfacial thermal resistance improves heat transport through the W–Cu composite.
Cu-modified tungsten interfaces increase the overall thermal conductivity of a W–Cu composite relative to an unmodified control.
Cu-modified tungsten interfaces preserve mechanical durability relative to a conventionally sintered W–Cu composite.
Cu-modified tungsten interfaces preserve irradiation resistance relative to a conventionally sintered W–Cu composite.
Standard W–Cu composites possess structural integrity and irradiation stability that can be maintained after interfacial modification.
The predicted benefits should persist under cyclic thermal loads and irradiation typical of fusion-reactor joints and high-power heat-dissipation applications.
Processing variations outside the stated application conditions may alter the benefits of Cu interfacial modification.
Thermal cycling from 77 K to 300 K can be used to compare modified and control composites.
A greater than 10% thermal-conductivity improvement over the control is the proposed threshold for a successful result.
